orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from the October 21, 2016 summary-judgment dismissal.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly fell while ascending the interior stairs of defendants’ building on December 19, 2013. Her deposition did not identify what caused the fall.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants established through plaintiff’s deposition that she could not identify the cause of the fall; she raised no triable issue, leaving negligent causation speculative.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendants submitted plaintiff’s deposition, which demonstrated inability to identify the cause of her fall.

quality.notes: Case-specific text says fell while ascending stairs without establishing a slip or trip. General slip/trip legal language does not supply the mechanism. Review is not based solely on failure to identify a negligent cause, which alone would not defeat eligibility. Building attribution also does not explicitly establish private ownership/control or use. Keep both unresolved scope reasons and a null binary label while recording the unambiguous affirmance. May 2014 is commencement, not the accident date. No specific hazard, injured role or defendant legal role is supplied.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
On December 19, 2013, the plaintiff allegedly sustained injuries when she fell while ascending the interior staircase of the defendants' building.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Walker, J.), dated October 21, 2016, which granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
After discovery, the defendants moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, contending that the plaintiff could not identify the cause of her fall.

Here, the defendants established their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by submitting, among other things, the plaintiff's deposition testimony, which demonstrated that she could not identify the cause of her fall
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact.
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from the order entered on or about October 1, 2018 dismissing claims against Diana and Todd Levy.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted Diana and Todd Levy’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint against them.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly tripped on the step from the living room of defendants’ apartment to the balcony. She testified that she had not looked down at the threshold, which required stepping down to the balcony floor.

legal_issues.finding: The court relied in part on evidence of no prior complaints or accidents concerning the step; the source does not identify the format of that evidence.
Photographs showed the metal threshold and step clearly visible through their shine and contrast with the darker balcony floor, defeating the claimed optical confusion.
The expert’s claimed optical-confusion cause was belied by photographs; plaintiff had testified that she did not look down at the threshold.
Plaintiff’s expert’s optical-confusion opinion was contradicted by record photographs.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff testified that she did not look down at the step-down threshold.
Record photographs showed a shiny, lighter-gray threshold and step contrasting with the balcony floor; they contradicted the expert’s optical-confusion opinion.
Plaintiff’s expert proposed optical confusion; the opinion was rejected based on the photographs. No expert specialty or submission format is specified.
The opinion identifies evidence of no prior complaints or accidents without specifying its form.

quality.notes: The actual step connects the living room and balcony of defendants’ apartment, supporting private residential control without assuming legal title. Stair hazard denotes the alleged step condition, not a missing handrail. Plaintiff’s relationship to defendants and accident date are unstated. Her failure to look down is not converted into a separate comparative-fault holding. No distinct constructive-notice inspection/timing analysis, trivial-defect finding or categorical lack-of-inherent-danger holding is inferred. One appealed order disposes of claims against the moving defendants; other named parties do not establish mixed relief.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, New York County (Arlene P. Bluth, J.), entered on or about October 1, 2018, which, inter alia, granted the motion of defendants Diana Levy and Todd Levy for summary judgment dismissing the complaint as against them, unanimously affirmed, without costs.

Summary judgment was properly granted in this action where plaintiff alleges that she was injured when, while walking from the living room in defendants' apartment to the balcony, she tripped and fell on the step leading to the balcony.

The evidence shows that there were no prior accidents or complaints about the step before plaintiff fell, and she testified that she did not look down at the threshold between the living room and the balcony, which required her to step down onto the balcony's floor

The opinion of plaintiff's expert that the balcony's step caused her optical confusion before the accident is belied by the photographs in the record that show a metal threshold and step that are shiny and clearly visible due to the fact that they are a lighter shade of gray than the balcony floor

Defendants established lack of actual notice, and plaintiff raised no triable issue.

quality.notes: Ownership and residential premises are explicit. Other injured role denotes the stated resident status without assuming tenancy or ownership; other hazard preserves wax rather than labeling it water or grease. evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is granted.
On October 17, 2015, the plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell while she was descending an interior staircase in the apartment building where she lived.

orders.description: Board’s limited appeal from the order entered on or about December 12, 2022 denying dismissal against it.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied the Board of Managers’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint against it.

facts.factual_summary: While working in a commercial basement parking garage within a condominium building, plaintiff allegedly slipped on water from ceiling drainpipes. The board disputed whether drainpipes were present above the accident site and whether they were common elements for which it was responsible.

legal_issues.finding: The board did not rule out responsibility under the declaration/by-laws for alleged pipes serving the entire building; it failed to establish absence of a maintenance duty.
Failure to exclude common-element pipes at the site prevented the board from establishing noncreation; this was an initial-burden failure, not proof of a pipe leak or negligent creation.
The court expressly found defendant had not established lack of constructive notice; the appeal’s creation-focused argument did not supply the missing showing. No inspection/timing details are given.
Expert and manager submissions did not eliminate factual issues about ceiling pipes and the alleged water source.
The board’s expert affidavit, together with manager testimony, did not eliminate issues about whether drainpipes existed above the accident location.

evidence_discussed.description: Board’s expert affidavit asserted absence of drainpipes over the site but did not eliminate factual issues; no specialty or method is stated.
Resident manager’s testimony likewise failed to eliminate factual issues about ceiling drainpipes.
Condominium declaration and by-laws assign responsibility for common elements, including pipes serving the entire building; the classification of the alleged pipes was not resolved.

quality.notes: The commercial garage unit within the condominium and declaration/by-law allocation of common-element control support private premises; no legal title is inferred. Disputed responsibility for particular pipes does not establish a public-property boundary. Working at the site alone does not establish employee rather than contractor status or identify an employer, so injured role remains unclear. Accident date is unstated. The limited appealed denial is fully affirmed; other parties do not create extra orders. Preserve both initial-burden failure and the alternative sufficient-opposition statement. No actual-notice, completed inspection, proven leak or expert specialty is inferred. Apply unchanged rules to this preliminary test-period case.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, New York County (Shlomo S. Hagler, J.), entered on or about December 12, 2022, which, to the extent appealed from as limited by the briefs, denied defendant Board of Managers of 1 Rector Park Condominium's (Board of Managers) motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint as against it, unanimously affirmed, without costs.
Plaintiff claims that, while working in the commercial parking garage unit of defendant's building, he slipped and fell on water which allegedly leaked from ceiling drainpipes.

Defendant did not demonstrate that it had no duty to maintain the accident site in accordance with the condominium's declaration and by-laws, which provide that defendant is responsible for "general common elements," including pipes and plumbing in the building that service the entire building

Defendant never specified which of the ceiling drain pipes in the basement garage did not service the entire building so as not to constitute "general common elements," and thus failed to establish it had no duty to maintain the alleged pipes that caused the accident

Defendant relied on the affidavit of its expert and the resident manager's testimony to assert that there were no drainpipes above the accident site. This evidence, however, did not eliminate triable issues of fact.
Defendant also failed to demonstrate that it did not create the alleged dangerous condition or have constructive notice of its existence.
On appeal, defendant only addresses the issue of whether it created the alleged dangerous condition.

Moreover, because defendant failed to demonstrate the absence of general common element drainpipes at the accident site, defendant failed to show that such alleged drainpipes did not create the dangerous condition.

Finally, because defendant failed to meet its summary judgment burden, of eliminating material issues of fact for trial, the burden never shifted to plaintiff to submit evidentiary facts or material raising a triable issue of fact
Even were we to find that defendant met its burden on the motion, we would find that plaintiff raised triable issues of fact requiring a trial of this negligence cause of action.

orders.description: Plaintiffs’ appeal from the December 19, 2012 order granting defendants’ dismissal motions.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendants’ motions for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on clear ice on the driveway of the house owned by the Solaros, for whom she worked. Contractor Doerr had last plowed snow under a verbal agreement more than a week earlier; plaintiff and Maria Solaro described no observed ice before the fall, including earlier that day.

legal_issues.finding: The snow-removal contractor established that he owed plaintiffs no duty.
Doerr established noncreation. The later snow-pile melt/refreeze theory was unpreserved and, alternatively, speculative and unsupported.
Pre-fall testimony, including earlier that day, supported defendants’ showing of no observable prior ice; the contrary affidavit and speculative recurring-ice theory did not raise a triable issue.
The new theory of recurrent ice from snow mounds was unpreserved and alternatively speculative, unsupported by evidence or climatological records and contrary to earlier-ice testimony.
The proposed causal chain from piled snow through melt runoff to driveway ice was rejected as speculative and unsupported, not established as an accident fact.
Doerr’s snow-removal agreement with the owners did not establish a duty to plaintiffs; the court also found noncreation under its cited Espinal framework.
Plaintiff’s opposing affidavit contradicted prior testimony; the new recurring-condition theory was unpreserved, and the court alternatively addressed its evidentiary insufficiency.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff and owner Maria Solaro described no observed prior ice; plaintiff’s opposing affidavit was rejected as directly contradictory to her earlier testimony.
The court states that climatological records did not support the melt/recurrence theory; it does not identify particular records or their contents.
A verbal snow-plowing agreement with the owners is described, with the last plowing more than a week before the fall; no written contract is claimed.

quality.notes: House and actual driveway ownership are explicit. Other location captures the driveway. Plaintiff worked for the Solaros; no occupation or work arrangement details are inferred. Accident date is unstated. One order granted multiple motions; all appealed relief is affirmed. Doerr’s noncreation/no-duty findings are specific to him. Lack of earlier observed ice is not a separate express actual-notice ruling, nor a storm-in-progress holding. No prior snow piles, melt/refreeze sequence or recurring hazard is treated as established. Climatological evidence is described only as nonsupporting, without inventing a missing report or independent weather check.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, Bronx County (Barry Salman, J.), entered December 19, 2012, which granted defendants’ motions for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, unanimously affirmed, without costs.
Plaintiff Sandra Paucar alleges that she slipped and fell on a patch of clear ice located on the driveway of a house owned by defendants Patrice and Maria Solaro, for whom she worked.
The snow had been last plowed by defendant Doerr, pursuant to a verbal agreement with the Solaros, more than one week earlier.

Defendants established their entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by submitting, inter alia, plaintiff’s testimony that she had not seen any icy condition on the driveway prior to her fall, including earlier that day, and Maria Solaro’s testimony that she did not observe an icy condition when she left the house that morning
Additionally, defendant Doerr established that he did not create the alleged condition and owed plaintiffs no duty
In opposition, plaintiffs failed to raise a triable issue of fact as her affidavit directly contradicted her earlier testimony

Plaintiff’s new theory, that the snow removal contractor’s method of piling snow in mounds, which then melted and caused water to run down the sloped driveway, creating the subject condition, which was a recurring condition, is unpreserved

In any event, the contention that the snow removal methods created a recurring condition is speculative, unsupported by the evidence or by climatological records, and contrary to the testimony which established a lack of any prior ice condition.
